articles.title: Terra indígena no PA registra 50 dias seguidos de queimadas | G1
articles.standfirst: Indígenas Parakanã, da TI Apyterewa, relatam cenário com morte de animais por invasores armados. Dados do ISA revelam até 104 focos de calor em um único dia. Ibama cita risco de conflito.
articles.summary: Indígenas Parakanã relatam cenário com morte de animais por invasores armados. Dados do ISA revelam até 104 focos de calor em um único dia. Ibama cita risco de conflito.
articles.body:
A Terra Indígena (TI) Apyterewa, localizada em São Félix do Xingu , no Pará, enfrenta uma onda de queimadas provocada por invasores , segundo os indígenas. O território, habitado pelo povo Parakanã, está sob chamas há 50 dias consecutivos e os indígenas estão em campo tentando combater as chamas .

Diante do cenário, o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) cobrou explicações urgentes do Ibama e do Corpo de Bombeiros Militar (CBMPA) sobre a falta de efetivo no combate aos incêndios florestais.

Vídeos gravados pelos indígenas mostram animais mortos pelo fogo , gravado no dia 5 de setembro, e um cavalo alvo de tiros por invasores , na segunda-feira (21) - ( assista ao vídeo acima ).

O órgão ambiental disse, em nota, que o caso é monitorado e o combate às chamas segue em curso - ( veja o posicionamento completo ao final da reportagem ). O CBMPA não se manifestou.

Um monitoramento do Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), com a plataforma da rede Xingu +, revela uma escalada no número de focos de incêndios florestais.

Focos de incêndio e mortes de animais são registrados por indígenas Parakanã, na Terra Indígena Apyterewa, no Pará. — Foto: Reprodução / Instituto Socioambiental

De acordo com o analista de geoprocessamento Ricardo Abad, entre os dias 1º e 21 de setembro, não houve um único dia sem registro de fogo na reserva . Somente neste período de 21 dias, foram detectados 687 focos de calor .

Se considerado o histórico recente, a TI Apyterewa queima sem trégua desde o dia 4 de agosto. O ápice do desastre ambiental ocorreu no último dia 19 de setembro , quando o território registrou o recorde histórico de 104 focos de calor em apenas 24 horas.

Outros dias também registraram altíssima liberação de energia radiativa (FRP), indicador que mede a intensidade do fogo, com destaque para o dia 14 de setembro e 20 de setembro.

A região afetada pelo fogo vinha sendo monitorada após a retirada de invasores, como grileiros e criadores de gado que ocupavam o território ilegalmente.

A TI Apyterewa tem 773 mil hectares, área pouco maior que a cidade de Goiânia (GO), é uma das áreas mais pressionadas pelo desmatamento no país . A reserva passou por um processo recente de desocupação , com a expulsão de invasores, com objetivo de garantir o direito originário e a segurança do povo Parakanã.

Enquanto o fogo avança sobre a floresta, os indígenas Parakanã relatam um cenário de completo abandono.

Segundo relatos da comunidade, a situação na região é precária e, até esta quarta-feira (23), nenhum órgão ambiental ou de segurança pública esteve no local para auxiliar diretamente no combate às chamas.

"Não tem bombeiros aqui. A situação está muito difícil e muitos animais da floresta já morreram queimados", lamentou um dos indígenas, que preferiu não se identificar.

Sem equipamentos adequados e treinamento, os próprios moradores tentam conter o avanço do fogo para proteger as aldeias.

A situação levou o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) a intervir. Em comunicação enviada ao Instituto Tato'a, entidade que acompanha a situação dos indígenas, o MPF informou que reiterou, em caráter de urgência, a cobrança de informações ao Ibama/Prevfogo e ao 31º Grupamento Bombeiro Militar de São Félix do Xingu.

O órgão pediu que as instituições apresentem as medidas emergenciais que estão sendo adotadas para conter o incêndio na TI Apyterewa. O comando dos bombeiros locais também foi acionado diretamente para que envie equipes de reforço à região.

Procurado pela reportagem, o Ibama informou, em nota, que a requisição do MPF trata das ações de prevenção e combate aos incêndios na TI Apyterewa. O órgão justificou a complexidade da operação citando o clima de tensão na área.

"Em 26 de agosto, a Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) acionou a Força Nacional para atuação tanto no combate ao fogo, quanto na proteção das equipes em atividade no local, visto que a TI passou a ser considerada zona de alto risco em razão de conflitos armados recorrentes."

O Ibama destacou ainda que a situação é monitorada pelo Centro Integrado Multiagências de Coordenação Operacional (Ciman) Federal e afirmou que "o combate às chamas segue em curso na região".

O g1 também procurou o Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Pará para esclarecer a falta de equipes na linha de frente denunciada pelos indígenas, mas não havia obtido resposta até a publicação desta reportagem.

articles.title: What happened to YouTuber Jenna Marbles? Where she is today after leaving her 20M subscribers behind
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Jenna Marbles built one of YouTube’s most recognisable careers by turning everyday moments into comedy that millions of people loved. But in June 2020.
articles.body: Jenna Marbles built one of YouTube’s most recognisable careers by turning everyday moments into comedy that millions of people loved. But in June 2020, the internet star walked away from the platform at the height of her popularity. Six years later, fans still wonder what happened to the creator who once had nearly 20 million subscribers. While Marbles has kept her life largely private, rare updates from people close to her have offered a glimpse into her world beyond social media.Jenna Marbles built a YouTube career before choosing privacyBorn Jenna Nicole Mourey, Marbles became a household name in the early days of YouTube. Her humour felt personal, chaotic and refreshingly relatable. She launched her channel on July 17, 2010, with “How to Trick People Into Thinking You’re Good Looking,” a comedy video that went on to attract 72 million views.Her channel grew into a major online destination, collecting nearly two billion views and more than 20 million subscribers at its peak. Marbles also earned a Shorty Award, received several Streamy Award nominations and appeared in television shows and films.For years, her videos were part of the internet’s weekly routine. That made her sudden departure in 2020 especially significant for longtime fans.Why Jenna Marbles left YouTube and what she is doing nowOn June 25, 2020, Marbles uploaded a tearful farewell video titled “A Message.” She addressed criticism over older content, including a video featuring her imitation of Nicki Minaj and material that viewers criticised as racially offensive.Marbles apologised and acknowledged the impact of her past videos. “I’ve tried my best to grow up and be a better person,” she told viewers.She also explained her decision to remove or make several videos private, saying, “For now, I just can’t exist on this channel.”The creator did not rule out a return, but she made clear that stepping away was necessary. “I think I’m just going to move on from this channel for now. I don’t know if that’s forever. I don’t know how long it’s going to be. I want to make sure that the things that I put into the world are not hurting anyone.”Since then, Marbles has maintained a remarkably low public profile. She has not resumed regular YouTube uploads or built a visible presence on Instagram or TikTok. Still, a few personal milestones have reached fans.In December 2022, her longtime partner, Julien Solomita, announced that they had married, sharing photos from their wedding. The couple also faced the loss of their beloved chihuahua, Mr. Marbles, who died in December 2025 at age 17.A rare update arrived in February 2026, when friend Rosanna Pansino spoke about Marbles on a podcast. “She got married, she spends time with dogs, I heard, volunteering. Last time I saw her was at [Safiya [Nygaard]] and [Tyler [Williams]’s] wedding.”While the details remain limited, Marbles appears to have built a quieter life away from the audience that once followed her every upload. For fans hoping for a comeback, there is no confirmed return. For now, her absence seems to be a choice she continues to make.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says
articles.summary: The UK could act as "an honest broker" on AI and other global challenges, the prime minister tells world leaders at the UN.
articles.body:
The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation, including from Russia, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation".

The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.

Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.

In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign.

"The Kremlin spends around £1.3bn each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly.

"They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.

"We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.

"On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'

He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.

To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.

The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".

There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham.

When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".

Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".

Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting

Before becoming prime minister, Burnham had said relatively little about how AI should be regulated.

Since taking power in July, Burnham's government has stressed the need for international cooperation to combat the risks, as well as harness the potential benefits of the technology, warning that further regulation and legislation may be needed.

In his speech, Burnham described the most advanced "Frontier AI" as "one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age".

He told world leaders AI would be "key to economic growth" but also a "multiplier of risk".

The prime minister added: "We've all heard the warnings – which we must heed. I know how worried people are. So we have to rise to this moment."

Burnham said the "UK has a unique position as an honest broker", with close ties to the US and the European Union.

He also highlighted the UK's "world-leading" AI Security Institute, which was established under Conservative Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and tests major AI models to improve their safety before they are released publicly.

He pledged to put AI "at the heart of the UK's G20 Presidency next year", when leaders of the world's biggest economies will gather in Manchester.

Burnham said the UK would work towards agreeing a set of global principles and standards to ensure transparency, access to AI models, and that development happens safely.

He added that this would "bring together welcome initiatives from others", such as a proposal from Norway this week.

The declaration - which has the support of more than 20 countries, including Germany, Canada and Ireland - calls for AI to remain under human control and for mandatory pre-release testing of frontier models.

However, it has not been signed by the US and China, which dominate AI development, or the UK.

Former cabinet minister Darren Jones, who served as chief secretary to Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, called on the prime minister to sign the declaration and offer to broker an agreement with the US on its implementation.

He argued there "should be a landing zone to agree mandatory testing", without undermining competitive advantage between companies and nations.

The UK AI Security Institute's testing of AI models is currently on a voluntary basis and AI company Anthropic reportedly refused to submit its latest model for testing.

Downing Street said officials had made clear in recent discussions with AI leaders that the government expects "full and total visibility of model developments".

The prime minister has acknowledged that while developers have made significant commitments on transparency, nothing is off the table to keep the public safe, including legislation.

Meanwhile, the government has announced a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

The Liberal Democrats and the Green Party have been putting pressure on the government to take further action on AI safety.

However, any international efforts to regulate AI would need the cooperation of the US and China.

In his own address earlier, US President Donald Trump rejected "any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI.

Trump has dismissed warnings of AI destroying humanity as "a hoax" and rejected the idea of a global scheme to control the technology.

"We're going to encourage it, not rein it in," he told the UN General Assembly.

Earlier in the day, Burnham and Trump had met, although Downing Street's statement on the meeting did not mention that they discussed AI.

AI poses huge risks to national security without guardrails, minister says

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Out to celebrate her birthday with a friend after visiting Kalkaji Temple, a 17-year-old girl from Faridabad was allegedly raped by three m.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Out to celebrate her birthday with a friend after visiting Kalkaji Temple, a 17-year-old girl from Faridabad was allegedly raped by three men posing as cops in Aastha Kunj Park near the bustling Nehru Place Monday evening. Police arrested one accused after an exchange of fire Tuesday morning and two others soon after.The girl, a student of Class XI, had gone to the park with a male friend, also 17, after visiting the temple around 7pm. They entered the park from a gate that’s close to Lotus Temple. Their nightmare began unfolding when the three men in plainclothes allegedly approached them and began intimidating them. They told them they were minors and doing something “wrong” and that their parents would be informed. They said a case would be registered and threatened to call the PCR, police said.They then allegedly manhandled and slapped the girl’s friend before taking her away to a secluded part of the park. Police said one of the men, Asif, threatened her with a firearm and a knife and raped her. The other two, Hemant and Mukesh, then allegedly took turns to rape her. The three men then fled after threatening the girl and her friend. The incident happened between 7.30pm and 8pm.One of accused arrested after exchange of fireThe girl called the PCR around 8.45pm and a team from Amar Colony police station, about 2km away, rushed to the spot. Police recorded the girl’s statement.Joint commissioner of police (southern range) Vijay Kumar said she was examined at AIIMS and crime and FSL teams inspected the scene. Some used condoms were found on the spot.A case was registered under BNS sections 70(2) for gang rape; 61(2) for criminal conspiracy; 115(2) for voluntarily causing hurt; and 351(3) for criminal intimidation along with sections 6 and 17 of Pocso Act.Police formed teams to trace the accused. Clues provided by the girl about the clothes the men were wearing and the names with which they were addressing each other proved critical in helping police make headway. With the help of some local enquiries and CCTV footage from the vicinity, where Hemant and Mukesh, who are brothers, were spotted, police were soon on the trail of the criminals.A breakthrough came around 6am Tuesday when a team received information about Asif having been spotted near DM Office Road in Amar Colony and laid a trap, said an officer.When police finally intercepted Asif and asked him to surrender, they said he fired three rounds. One bullet hit head constable Rajesh, who was wearing a bulletproof jacket. Rajesh then fired two rounds, one of which hit Asif in his right leg, police said.He was taken to AIIMS Trauma Centre for treatment. As Asif began singing, police tracked down Hemant and Mukesh and arrested them later in the day.Police said Asif is a wholesaler of vegetables at Okhla mandi. He is married and has a daughter. Hemant’s father, advocate J R Dhankar, has told police that his son is a lawyer, a claim that police are verifying. Mukesh is a BSc student.Dhankar has accused police of framing his sons. “One of my sons is an advocate practising at Saket courts while the other is pursuing BSc in mathematics. Police picked them up from their home in Sriniwaspuri early in the morning without informing us. Their statements were taken forcibly. This is a conspiracy. They did not know Asif. They were at home Monday and did not go out,” he alleged.Police, however, claim that the three men have said during interrogation that they had met each other about three months ago.Aastha Kunj, unlike its name which spells hope, has gained notoriety over the years for lack of security. Over the past few years, several cases of robberies, snatchings and harassment have been reported here.The park, which was meant to serve as a link to Kalkaji Temple, Baha’i Temple (Lotus Temple) and Iskcon Temple, and also gives access to Nehru Place District Centre and the extended food and entertainment zones, is managed by DDA.It is spread across 140 acres and has 29 entry points. articles.title: US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
articles.summary: Under the draft laws, tech firms face fines if they do not give users the option to switch off algorithms.
articles.body:
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".

Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.

In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.

"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.

The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.

An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.

"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."

The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".

Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.

The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.

On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.

"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.

"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."

US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".

This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

articles.title: Haze-choked Indonesia records more than 170,000 respiratory cases
articles.summary: More than 40,000 of the cases – which range from mild coughs to pneumonia – involve toddlers.
articles.body:
Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks .

More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.

Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory.

Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say.

"From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday.

"Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires."

Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October.

This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino , which has fuelled extremely dry conditions.

The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons.

Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.

The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia.

The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry.

The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans.

Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died.

Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province.

"This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time.

Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts.

Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice.

In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month.

Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October.

"October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can."

The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.

articles.title: Super El Niño: California declares emergency as Hurricane Polo remains Category 5 off Mexico
articles.summary: US News: US federal forecasts put the chance of a very strong El Niño above 90% this autumn and winter, with a 75% probability that the event could reach histo.
articles.body: US federal forecasts put the chance of a very strong El Niño above 90% this autumn and winter, with a 75% probability that the event could reach historic strength. California has declared a state of emergency ahead of the winter weather threat, while Hurricane Polo remains a Category 5 storm off Mexico.California Gov Gavin Newsom declared the emergency on Monday to mobilize resources before the El Niño peaks this winter. The order allows the state to position resources in advance and coordinate preparations for severe weather.California is likely to be among the US areas most exposed to the unusually strong climate cycle. Previous strong El Niño events have frequently brought damaging conditions to the state, while studies have associated them with above-normal precipitation, Cable News Network (CNN) reported.The effects are already being seen along the California coast, where El Niño has pushed sea levels higher. As the event reaches its expected winter peak, the state could face coastal flooding, heavy rainfall at lower elevations and mountain snow.Scientists regard widespread flooding along the coast as close to certain. El Niño can also add energy to waves generated by Pacific storms, increasing the risk of coastal erosion and closures on key transport links.Those coastal risks do not depend entirely on the path taken by major Pacific storms. El Niño itself raises coastal water levels, adding to sea-level rise already linked to climate change.The El Niño also coincides with the peak of an 18-year astronomical high-tide cycle. Patrick Barnard, research director at the Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at the University of California, Santa Cruz, said the cycle will push King Tides above their usual levels.Barnard said studies have found wave energy from Pacific storms to be about 30% higher during El Niño years. The increase reached as much as 50% during the 2015-16 event.He said a projected rise of about 15cm to 30cm in coastal water levels during the current El Niño could put another 170,000 people and $60 billion in property at risk compared with a non-super El Niño year.Polo remains Category 5 after winds peak at 285kmphOff Mexico, Hurricane Polo remained at Category 5 strength on Tuesday after rapidly intensifying amid favourable atmospheric conditions and warmer water associated with the super El Niño.Polo's sustained winds peaked at about 285kmph at 3pm CST, when its minimum central pressure fell to 892mb, according to the National Hurricane Center. By 9pm, sustained winds had eased to about 270kmph and the hurricane was drifting northeast at about 2kmph. Its minimum central pressure had risen to 905mb, but it remained an “extremely dangerous” Category 5 storm.Between Monday and Tuesday morning, Polo's winds increased by about 175kmph, rising from around 80kmph as a tropical storm to about 260kmph at Category 5 strength.A storm meets the threshold for extreme rapid intensification when its wind speed rises by at least about 95kmph within 24 hours. The centre called Polo's rate of strengthening “truly remarkable” and said it was among the fastest recorded in the eastern Pacific.For comparison, Hurricane Patricia set the eastern Pacific 24-hour intensification record in 2015 with an increase of about 195kmph. In 2023, Hurricane Otis gained about 170kmph in 21 hours before hitting and devastating Acapulco.California, southwest Mexico face flood threatCalifornia could see flooding, mudslides and landslides as heavier precipitation combines with stronger storm waves.Newsom's emergency order directs agencies to prepare roads and other infrastructure, coordinate public-safety measures with local and tribal governments and pre-position equipment for flood response and snow removal. The California National Guard is also being readied for flood-response, search-and-rescue, engineering and logistics operations.A Tropical Storm Warning was in effect along Mexico's southwest coast from Tecpan de Galeana to Punta San Telmo. Polo's core was expected to remain offshore, but heavy rain posed a risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides in Guerrero and Michoacán.Mexican authorities suspended classes in affected areas along the Pacific coast, the Associated Press reported.Reuters reported that authorities were monitoring the risk of rivers overflowing and had urged residents to stay away from flooded areas, secure loose outdoor items and plan routes to higher ground.Guerrero and Michoacán were forecast to receive about 8cm to 15cm of rain through Thursday, with isolated totals of up to 20cm. articles.title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
articles.summary: A concerning number of patients are reporting problems from treatment abroad, say doctors.
articles.body:
Warning: Graphic images and descriptions of surgery

"Everyone made it out to be so easy, but my face felt like it was on fire and there was a horrible smell of burning skin," says Nikita Morgan, as she describes her eyelid surgery.

She decided to get a blepharoplasty, or a "bleph", removing skin from just above the eyes - after seeing videos about it on social media. Even though she was given a local anaesthetic, Nikita felt extreme pain.

Oculoplastic surgeons - doctors specialising in surgery around the eyes - say a concerning number of patients are reporting problems from cheap bleph surgery, typically carried out abroad.

They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.

Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.

As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight.

UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad.

Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400).

Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650).

She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".

The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.

It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.

The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.

Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.

She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before.

"I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."

Faceland says all patients have consultations and sign consent forms before procedures, to ensure they are "well informed and well prepared".

It added that Nikita's doctor had said Nikita was "very anxious and uncertain" during her procedure "which can influence the perception of pain".

Within hours, a "traumatised" Nikita was boarding a plane home. Flying on the same day of surgery is not advised by medical experts as well as Faceland, but she saw lots of people doing it on social media.

"I was struggling to see," says Nikita, "if I looked up, my stitches would bleed so it was like I was crying blood."

She really regrets flying on the same day as her surgery and advises others not to.

In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years.

Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland.

One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved.

The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says.

Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics.

Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs.

Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened.

Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad.

The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us.

The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E.

"When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony."

In the days after, Laura was communicating with her doctor from Faceland and, on several occasions, she offered to fly back for assessment.

"I was crying, literally begging: 'You can't leave me like this'," she says.

But Faceland told her the best course of action was seeking treatment local to her.

Laura was referred to an NHS eye specialist who said "excessive skin" had been removed.

How did Laura feel about the NHS picking up the cost of fixing her cheap surgery?

"I feel guilty... People will think 'it's your own fault', but I would never have gone had I known what could happen."

Faceland says it cannot comment in detail about Laura's case because she is pursuing legal action against the company.

As a goodwill gesture an independent complaints committee that works with Faceland offered Laura €175 (£150), which she has rejected.

UK surgeons tell us that, when they have seen patients with blepharoplasty complications over the past 12 months, those people have, in most cases, been treated abroad.

The most common issue following overseas procedures has been people not being able to close their eyes properly, according to a survey for the BBC, to which 63 members of the British Oculoplastic Surgery Society (Bopss) in the UK and Ireland responded.

"Removing too much skin from the eyelid is dangerous because it leaves the eye exposed to the elements," explains consultant ocuplastic surgeon, Colin Vize, who is on the Bopss executive committee. "Correction can be difficult and expensive."

He likens eyelids to "a pair of curtains". When you open them there needs to be a pleat, so when you close them there is enough skin to cover the eyeball.

Other issues from overseas procedures reported by the Bopss members include scarring, uneven eyes and wounds opening up.

Surgeons say they also saw patients with complications after having been treated by unregistered UK practitioners, including blepharoplasties that had been carried out in living rooms.

On Christmas Day 2024, Caryn Harte woke up struggling to see.

It was days after her bleph surgery at Faceland's Amsterdam clinic, her swollen left eye was weeping blood, and the wounds above both eyes had started to open.

"I was terrified I was going to lose my sight over a bit of excess skin," she says.

Caryn went straight to A&E, seeing no point in calling Faceland because it was too far away.

Doctors later reassured her she would keep her vision, but her face was badly infected. She was prescribed antibiotics and required hospital check-ups.

The BBC has seen emails that show Caryn contacted Faceland twice, to report what had happened, and that she received a short reply 12 days later. A few further emails followed, but Caryn says she has not heard from the company since.

Faceland maintains it "did not leave her without support or follow-up during the aftercare process".

It says it is sorry if patients felt insufficiently supported by its teams or experienced complications.

Like Caryn, Laura and Nikita, patients we have spoken to who have had cheap eyelid surgery abroad say limited aftercare is their biggest complaint.

"Aftercare for the typical bleph should be available to a patient 24/7," says Vize. "If your surgeon is hundreds of miles away, the ability to provide care with a sense of immediacy is impossible."

He also warns that patients should be aware that in some cases lower costs may mean lower standards.

A week after her surgery, Nikita removed her own stitches. She worked out what to do by watching TikTok videos.

"It makes you feel weak, like you're pulling something out of your skin," she says.

Faceland says patients are advised to consult its doctors about when to remove their stitches and are given information on how to do so. Nikita says she did not receive an aftercare pack or instructions.

The company also says patients can come back to a Faceland clinic to have stitches removed, but no-one we spoke to had done that.

Patients removing their own stitches is "a recipe for disaster", according to Vize, who says stitches should be taken out by a surgeon or a nurse to reduce the infection risk and the chance of wounds splitting open.

Nikita is mostly happy with her results, aside from a small scar, but she wants other people to learn from her experiences and fully understand the risks.

"If I'd had the money or if I hadn't listened to the spin on TikTok, I probably would have gone somewhere closer to home and not rushed into it," she says.

Nearly two years on, Caryn still has issues with her left eye, including some blurry vision and scarring.

Meanwhile, Laura fears she may have scars above both of her eyes for life.

"I tried to fix a problem that didn't really need fixing, and I've come back with a bigger problem that I need surgery for, and I can't afford that," she says. "It's pretty devastating."

articles.title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
articles.summary: The UN Population Fund also says there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriages.
articles.body:
There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).

One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence".

It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN.

Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed.

Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing

One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says.

Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023.

Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17.

"The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system".

While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire.

Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety.

Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable.

One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15.

"Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is."

The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women.

"We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad."

The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining.

The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war.

The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike.

Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point."

"If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home."

A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain."

Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms.

The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers.

This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%.

Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war.

"One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report.

Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes.

There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer.

articles.title: Rare glimpse inside Burslem theatre closed since 1998
articles.summary: A rare tour of Stoke-on-Trent's Queen's Theatre reveals growing hopes for its revival.
articles.body:
The first thing visitors notice is the door.

After 28 years shut, it creaks open to reveal a dark corridor where, as I joined the rare few taking a step inside, paint peels from walls and bare light bulbs hang from the ceiling.

But beyond the signs of decay lies a surprise: an ornate auditorium that has survived decades of neglect and is now at the centre of ambitious plans to bring one of a city's most treasured theatres back to life.

For Barry Green, stepping inside the Queen's Theatre in Stoke-on-Trent for the first time in years was a moment he will not forget.

One of about 100 people given a rare glimpse behind its doors, he said the hairs on the back of his neck stood up when he entered the auditorium.

The theatre holds special memories for him.

As a member of local punk-indie band Cock's Entry, named after a nearby walkway in Burslem, he once performed on its stage.

"Being able to play there was a privilege," he said.

Like many visitors, Green was struck not by how much the building had deteriorated, but by how much had survived.

"I expected pigeons in the rafters, but the ceiling is in good shape," he said.

"The structure looks great, far better than what I expected. It's far bigger than I expected because we went into nooks and crannies I'd never been in before."

Opened in 1911, the Queen's Theatre spent decades hosting plays, concerts and community events.

Among those to tread its boards was a young Robbie Williams, who appeared as the Artful Dodger in a production of Oliver! in 1988.

Since closing 28 years ago, the building has stood silent.

Today, campaigners hope to change that by transforming it into Kilmister Halls, a new entertainment venue honouring Motorhead frontman Lemmy, who was born in nearby Burslem.

Few understand the affection local people still have for the theatre better than Lindsey Glover.

Now a volunteer at Lemmy's Lounge, a community bar set up to support the project, she remembers working behind the bar during boxing promotions held at the venue towards the end of its life.

"It's an absolutely beautiful building," she said. "They don't make buildings like that anymore. The architecture, the marble, the work that must've gone into it."

Walking through the building today was bittersweet, she added.

"It's really sad when you walk through and you remember how it was, but it's also knowing that it is going to be reopened."

Glover recalled busy nights when the auditorium would fill with spectators for boxing events, bringing crowds back into the historic venue.

But, she believes, what lies ahead could eclipse even those memories.

After emerging from the theatre, many visitors continued their conversations in nearby pubs and bars, discussing the building's future and what its revival could mean for Burslem.

For Green, the excitement was impossible to ignore.

"Being my town makes it even more exciting," he said. "We walked out of there buzzing."

articles.title: Rare snails lay eggs on drive from Wales to Wingham Wildlife Park
articles.summary: The zoo near Canterbury says glutinous snails started laying eggs on their way to Kent.
articles.body:
A rare snail found in just one lake in the UK started laying eggs on its six-hour journey from Wales to Kent, as a zoo joined a nationwide effort to save the species.

Glutinous snails are no bigger than a fingertip and used to be widespread across UK water ways.

It is thought habitat disruption and environmental changes reduced their population to such an extent that they are only now found in Llyn Tegid , a lake in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia.

Wingham Wildlife Park near Canterbury has taken some of the wild population to breed and release into the wild. Samantha Eden, assistant curator, said the zoo started with six snails and recently started a new colony.

Despite their slow reputation, the breeding efforts are off to a flying start, Eden said.

"I brought 24 snails back from Wales at the start of July," she said.

"It was a six hour drive, and by the time I'd arrived back at the park I had about 12 egg pods in the carry containers that we were using. They'd laid eggs literally whilst we were driving.

"We started, with one of the ponds, with just six adult snails. We recently moved 130 babies out of that pond to start a new colony."

Hannah Ellins, head of reptiles and invertebrates, said: "We do a lot of work with exotics, but it's cool being able to help our animals here."

She added: "We'll keep breeding them and then hopefully we'll eventually then release them into the wild and help wild populations."

The scheme is part of a wider national effort to protect the very rare species.

Wingham Wildlife Park is joining Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released.

articles.title: Zelenskyy, after meeting Trump, says Ukraine ready for 'energy ceasefire' with Russia
articles.summary: Europe News: Ukraine is ready to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow agrees to stop striking Ukraine's power and other critical energy infrastructu.
articles.body: Ukraine is ready to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow agrees to stop striking Ukraine's power and other critical energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after meeting US President Donald Trump in New York.Zelenskyy said the proposal for an "energy ceasefire" was discussed as the two leaders held a 40-minute meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence had detected preparations for what he described as a major new Russian attack.Writing on X, Zelenskyy called his meeting with Trump "positive and productive" and said both countries wanted to end the war before winter."Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter. We discussed potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy," he added.Kyiv offers reciprocal energy truceSpeaking to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to stop hitting Russian energy targets, but only if Russia stopped its own attacks on Ukraine's energy network."We are ready for energy ceasefire," he said. "If they don’t want us to attack their diesel and refineries, and etc, we are ready – if they will not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating system, water supplies."Zelenskyy stressed that he had not agreed to unilaterally stop Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry.Trump had raised the issue of Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries before meeting Zelenskyy. The US president said the attacks had damaged Russian fuel-processing capacity and were also affecting diesel prices."It is a serious hit on the Russians. It’s also a serious hit on the price of diesel," Trump said.Trump said the two leaders would also discuss ways to end the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "I think it’s going to happen," he added.Previous energy deal failed to holdTrump said last week that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure. However, attacks resumed soon afterwards.Moscow had previously backed a US proposal for an energy moratorium, while also seeking measures covering Russian seaborne energy exports and sanctions.Zelenskyy, however, rejected any immediate discussion about easing sanctions against Russia while Ukrainian cities remained under attack.Following a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he wrote on Telegram that there could be no discussion of sanctions relief "when Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone attacks".He added that Ukrainian intelligence had detected preparations for another major Russian offensive."There’s intelligence right now that Russia is preparing a new ⁠massive attack against Ukraine," he wrote.Russia and Ukraine intensify energy strikesThe latest proposal comes after weeks of attacks by both sides on energy infrastructure and other strategic targets.Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian power, fuel and port facilities. Kyiv has also been preparing for further attacks on its energy network as winter approaches.On September 15, Ukrainian officials said Russia launched about 200 drones across the country. The attacks hit petrol stations in Kyiv as well as energy and port infrastructure in other areas.Ukraine has meanwhile stepped up its long-range drone campaign against Russia's oil industry. Its strikes have targeted refineries and other energy facilities as far as 3,000km from the Ukrainian border.A September 20 strike reportedly forced the Moscow oil refinery to stop crude processing. The refinery processed around 230,000 barrels of crude oil a day in 2024, according to industry sources cited by Reuters.The proposed energy ceasefire would therefore focus on a specific part of the wider conflict, rather than amounting to a broader halt in fighting.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Unjustifiable' Alderney Airport runway upgrade delays criticised
articles.summary: Delays and changes to the refurbishment project cause concern in Alderney.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised after a project to rebuild an island airport's runway were delayed.

The decision not to widen Alderney Airport's runway from 18m (59ft) to 23m (75ft) to meet regulatory guidelines and hold off on any work happening until 2028 has been criticised by islanders and aviation experts.

Giles Woodhouse, who travels from Alderney to the UK frequently, said the delay left question marks as to whether "living on this beautiful island was still viable".

Deputy Mark Helyar, President of the States' Trading Supervisory Board, said the project board was focused on delivering the government's direction to identify the lowest possible cost and most practical and pragmatic approach.

Earlier this year, plans to spend up to £24m on refurbishing the runway were passed by the States of Guernsey with the aim of starting the work in 2027.

Woodhouse, who is head of sales for clothing brand Gym Plus Coffee, said, for work, medical or family and friends connections, the air service being functional was "absolutely vital".

He said he felt "resigned exasperation" when the delay was announced.

Woodhouse said the continued delays also led to questions about whether the project would actually happen.

"With no concrete dates, it just feels really unjustifiable," Woodhouse added.

Geoff Blyth, an Alderney resident and flying instructor, said the decision not to widen the runway could have a big impact on the population of the island.

Blythe said if the director of civil aviation (DCA) did not accept the safety case put forward regarding the decision to keep the runway 18m wide, it could impose "restrictions when we have inclement weather".

The pilot added this would mean a lot more flight cancellations leading to "lost revenue" and a big impact on the hospital because of "wasted appointments".

"That's not good for anybody," Bylthe said.

The runway's current width of 18m is below the minimum 23m required for a runway longer than 800m (2,625ft) to achieve compliance with regulatory standards.

The States said "operations are currently permitted due to an 'alleviation' from the DCA" and the regulator had confirmed the alleviation could continue "provided a suitable safety case is presented" due to the type of aircraft which use the runway.

Jeannie Cameron, chairwoman of the Alderney Policy and Finance Commitee, said it was "incredibly frustrating" after delays dating back 10 years, a further delay of two years was being faced.

Cameron said a request was put forward to have an Alderney politician on the project's board so "we could have a voice but we were told no".

She added the States of Alderney "put forward two proposals which came in well under budget" of the initial £24 million plan.

"We still have not had a response to those," she said.

Of the decision not to widen the runway, Cameron said none of the politicians involved were airline or runway specialists so they needed to take advice.

Cameron said: "We need a timetable and the ability to ensure that those accountable are held to account."

Beth Chapman, community governor of St Anne's School, said the project's delay was "incredibly disappointing to hear".

Chapman added: "It needs to happen, it's just gone on and on and it can't carry on like this.

"Having an airline here isn't a luxury, it's a lifeline."

Heylar said the project board was "generally seeking regulatory alleviations where possible to minimise the amount of work needed".

"The project board is focussed on delivering the States direction which is to identify the lowest possible cost and most practical and pragmatic approach to maintain an operational aerodrome in Alderney," he added.

articles.title: A 1954 Superman lunchbox sold for $31,980, beating its $20,000 high estimate at auction
articles.summary: US News: A metal lunchbox from the early years of Superman merchandise has become one of the notable vintage toy sales of 2026. The 1954 Superman lunchbox, com.
articles.body: A metal lunchbox from the early years of Superman merchandise has become one of the notable vintage toy sales of 2026. The 1954 Superman lunchbox, complete with its matching Thermos and protective case, sold for $31,980 at Morphy Auctions’ Toys & General Collectables sale in June. The price was well above the auction house’s high estimate of $20,000, as per Morphy Auctions. Its value was tied to more than the Superman name. The lot brought together an early licensed lunchbox, original accessories and colourful period artwork, offering a surviving example of the kind of everyday object that carried comic-book characters into children’s lives during the 1950s.The 1954 Superman lunchbox turned a school essential into comic-book merchandiseThe lunchbox was manufactured by ADCO Liberty and released by Universal in 1954, when character-themed lunchboxes were beginning to establish themselves as a recognisable part of the children's market. Rather than being a plain container for a school meal, the metal box used lithographed artwork to turn the object itself into a piece of Superman merchandise.The auction lot included the Thermos as well as a protective case. That completeness helped distinguish it from a loose or incomplete example. The Superman graphics were also a major part of its visual identity, showing the Man of Steel in a confrontation with a giant gold robot against a city skyline.The Superman lunchbox stood out in a $1.8 million collectibles saleThe Superman piece was one of 1,362 lots offered during Morphy’s Toys & General Collectibles auction, held on June 2 and 3, 2026. The wider sale generated more than $1.8 million, with vintage toys, sports memorabilia, marbles and other collectibles competing for attention.The Superman lunchbox was not the most expensive item in the auction, but its final price put it firmly among the sale’s notable results. It also formed part of a strong showing for the lunchbox category, which auctioneer Dan Morphy said had broken records alongside the soldier and marble categories.Morphy Auctions had placed a high estimate of $20,000 on the Superman lunchbox that ultimately sold for $31,980. It was not simply a high-priced vintage toy appearing in a major sale. The bidding pushed the final figure substantially beyond the upper end of the published estimate.Character lunchboxes from the 1950s and 1970s drew strong auction pricesThe Superman result was part of a broader run of strong prices for vintage lunchboxes in the same auction. A mid-1950s Toppie the Elephant metal lithographed lunchbox sold for $16,605. It retained its matching Thermos, including the red cup lid, and came with two original Toppie companion books.A much later Underdog lunchbox, dating to around 1974, went further. The Leonard TTV metal example sold for $22,140 despite having some very mild surface scratches. Its condition was described as nearly mint overall, although the Thermos-Sew Thermos accompanying it was not original to the lunchbox.The Superman lot therefore sat in a wider group of character lunchboxes that attracted substantial prices. Its 1954 date, original Thermos and protective case gave it a different place within that group, while the artwork connected it directly with one of the best-known comic characters of the period.Superman was only one of several major auction resultsThe June sale had plenty of competition outside the lunchbox category. A 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card sold for $51,660, matching the price achieved by a circa-1893 W Britains Germanic boxed set of royal fusiliers. The auction house described both as joint top lots.The W Britains set contained eight foot figures and a mounted officer and was housed in its original box. A first-version 275-piece W Britains Types of the British Army No. 131 set also performed strongly, selling for $41,820.The baseball material continued with a complete unopened 1972 Topps Series 3 wax box containing 24 factory-sealed packs, or 240 cards in total. That lot sold for $35,670, as reported.Marbles provided another unexpected high pointMarbles were another major part of the sale. articles.title: Paid Rs 84,960 for '100% placement guarantee', got no job: MBA graduate wins refund
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Punjab has directed a educational institution to refund Rs 84,960 to an MBA graduate after the company fa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Punjab has directed a educational institution to refund Rs 84,960 to an MBA graduate after the company failed to provide the “100 percent guaranteed placement” promised while selling the course to the student. The commission also awarded Rs 10,000 compensation and Rs 5,000 litigation costs in an order passed on September 16, 2026.Why did the consumer approach the commission?According to the commission order, Harish Malhotra, an MBA graduate, enrolled in a six-month online training programme in AI in product management after seeing Eduinx Education Services Private Limited advertisement promising “100 percent guaranteed placement”. He paid Rs 84,960 through a credit card on July 12, 2025.The complainant completed the course and received a certificate on November 24, 2025. He alleged that despite repeated follow-ups, the company failed to provide the promised placement and kept giving revised timelines. He then approached the Gurdaspur district consumer commission seeking a refund of the course fee, along with compensation for mental agony, harassment, financial loss and loss of career continuity.He also claimed that he remained unemployed for over 10 months and sought Rs 6 lakh as compensation and Rs 30,000 towards litigation expenses.However, the Eduinx denied the allegations and said it was an upskilling and career-support platform, not an appointing authority. It argued that the “100 percent placement guarantee” referred to career preparation, profile optimisation and employer outreach, while final selection depended on employers.The company further claimed that the complainant had participated in recruitment processes involving companies including Cognizant, Capgemini and Innomick. It claimed he had declined job opportunities in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad because he preferred Gurugram or Delhi-NCR.Why did the commission hold Eduinx responsible?The bench comprising President Lalit Mohan Dogra and member B S Matharu observed that the company had accepted Rs 84,960 after promising that the programme carried a 100 percent placement guarantee. The bench noted that while Eduinx had shown evidence of recruitment efforts, it had not established that the promised placement commitment was fulfilled.The commission said there was a difference between offering interview opportunities and providing the placement that had been represented to the consumer.“The opposite parties cannot simultaneously rely upon the expression “100 percent placement guarantee” to induce a consumer to purchase the programme and, after the consumer has paid the consideration, interpret the same merely as a promise to forward his profile to employers and arrange interviews. If the service was in fact limited to providing interview opportunities and recruitment assistance, that limitation ought to have been clearly and prominently disclosed to the complainant at the time of enrolment,” the commission noted.The commission also rejected the company’s argument that the complainant's interview performance was responsible for the failure to secure a job. It noted that Eduinx had not produced interview assessments, ratings or communications from the employers showing that he was rejected on the basis of his performance.The bench said the WhatsApp conversations showed that some job opportunities had been communicated to Malhotra, but these did not amount to a definite employment offer or successful placement.“A mere suggestion of a vacancy cannot be equated with an employment offer as promised. Nor can a recruitment lead, screening call or interview be treated as equivalent to successful placement. Therefore, even after taking the WhatsApp conversations at their face value, the evidence falls short of establishing that the opposite parties fulfilled the substantive placement representation,” the commission further noted.The commission held that the failure to fulfil the placement commitment amounted to deficiency in service. It also held that the representation of “100 percent guaranteed placement”, without sufficiently clear conditions showing that it did not actually assure placement, amounted to an unfair trade practice.“If the opposite parties wished to make the guarantee conditional upon the complainant's performance in interviews, they were required to establish the existence and applicability of such conditions. A general assertion made after the dispute arose cannot substitute for a clear contractual qualification disclosed at the time of sale of the service. Accordingly, we hold that the opposite parties have failed to establish that the placement commitment was fulfilled and that such failure constitutes a shortcoming in the manner of performance of the service hired by the complainant” the commission concluded.The commission, however, rejected Malhotra’s claim for Rs 6 lakh towards financial loss and loss of career continuity, saying there was insufficient documentary evidence to establish the exact amount and direct connection with the company’s service.What did the commission order?The Gurdaspur district consumer commission directed Eduinx Education Services Pvt Ltd to:Refund Rs 84,960 to Malhotra.Pay Rs 10,000 as compensation for mental tension and harassment.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses.Make the payments jointly and severally within 45 days of receiving a copy of the order.Pay 9 percent annual interest on the Rs 84,960 refund from the date of deposit until actual realisation if the order is not complied with within 45 days.

articles.title: A Cartier watch was found inside a British charity-shop donation bag; it was authenticated as an 18-carat gold watch and sold for £9,766
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Cartier watch found in a bag of donated items at a British Heart Foundation shop in Hounslow was later identified as an 18-carat gold Cartier Tank F.
articles.body: A Cartier watch found in a bag of donated items at a British Heart Foundation shop in Hounslow was later identified as an 18-carat gold Cartier Tank Française. The luxury timepiece was sent for authentication before being listed online, where it attracted dozens of bids from potential buyers. It eventually sold for £9,766.66 in December 2022, becoming the charity’s highest-value online sale at the time. The unexpected discovery turned an ordinary donation into a substantial contribution to the British Heart Foundation’s charitable work.How the Cartier watch was found in a charity-shop donationThe watch arrived at the British Heart Foundation’s shop in Hounslow, west London, among a bag of donated belongings. Staff could not simply assume that the item was valuable, so it was sent to the charity’s Online Hub in Leeds for verification.According to UK Fundraising, the item was identified as a Cartier Tank Française made from 18-carat gold. The discovery was particularly striking because charity shops routinely receive large quantities of donated goods, making the valuable watch a unique find. It was then checked again by experts at an independent auction house, giving the charity further confirmation before it was offered for sale.What happened before the gold watch went on saleOnce the watch had been authenticated, the British Heart Foundation worked with Shopiago, its online selling partner, to reach buyers beyond the charity shop.Instead of placing the timepiece on a normal shop counter, the charity listed it on eBay, where it could be seen by a much wider audience. This gave the donation an opportunity to attract collectors and buyers interested in Cartier watches. As per The Independent, the watch reached the final price of £9,766.66 after 46 bids.The main attraction of Cartier Tank Française watchThe Cartier name added to the interest surrounding the discovery. Cartier watches have long been worn by well-known figures, including Diana, Princess of Wales, Jake Gyllenhaal, Angelina Jolie and Michelle Obama.UK Fundraising noted that Michelle Obama had worn a Cartier Tank Française and that the model appeared in her official White House portrait. These associations helped underline the popularity of the particular watch design, although the charity’s discovery was valuable because of the watch itself rather than its connection to any celebrity owner.The charity recorded its biggest online saleThe £9,766.66 sale became a record for the British Heart Foundation’s online operation at the time. UK Fundraising reported that the charity had sold 236,000 donated items online in 2021, showing how online selling had become an important part of its retail activity.Shopiago, which helped the BHF sell the watch online, also described the item as its most valuable single item sold through the platform at that point. The company said charities had sold 641,000 donated items online through Shopiago during the previous year.The sale therefore stood out not only because of the luxury watch but also because of what it showed about the potential value hidden within donated goods. The money went to the British Heart Foundation rather than back to the person who originally donated the watch.The charity had achieved significant sums from other unusual donations as well. UK Fundraising reported that a seven-inch vinyl demo of the Beatles’ Love Me Do had previously sold for £9,400, while a second-hand Mercedes-Benz E320 had brought in £7,502. The Cartier watch surpassed both of those figures to become the BHF’s record online sale at the time.For the charity, the discovery ultimately turned an ordinary donation into nearly £10,000 for its work. The BHF’s head of online retail, Richard Pallier, said that public donations were central to allowing the organisation to continue its work funding research into heart and circulatory disease. The story showed how a valuable object can pass unnoticed when it is mixed in with everyday donations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban
articles.summary: One of those killed is believed to be a pregnant woman, police said.
articles.body:
At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.

Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.

Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".

While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings".

"Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.

A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.

The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects.

South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.

In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.

Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.

Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.
